deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the surrounding pages). Γ(Σ) (also written Γ*(Σ)) is a combinatorial graph or cell complex attached to the 'space' of pseudo-line systems. A vertex D is a configuration, a 'carte' given by a system of pseudo-lines. Edges are elementary degenerations or deformations. An edge leaving D is a specialization, an edge arriving at D is a generalization, and there are also 'neutral' edges. Edges carry an orientation and an integer gradation.

For each D, Pol*(D) is the 'local polygon' (the link of D). Its vertices are the edges of Γ(Σ) at D, and its edges are graded. It carries an antipodal involution, and the previous page shows that specialization vertices are stable under antipody. P̂ol*(D) is the 'deployed' (unfolded) polygon, apparently obtained by subdividing each edge according to its gradation. For a specialization D → D' there is a specialization morphism Pol*(D) → Pol*(D'). The previous page states additivity constraints for it: the gradation of an arc equals the sum of the gradations of its pieces.

Page 24, left column. Grothendieck doubts that the oriented graded graph structure of Γ*(Σ) alone can tell, among the edges issuing from D, which correspond to 'pseudo-specializations' (specialization triangles) and which do not. The incident edges are often generalizations. He notes that the distinction can be recovered once the specialization morphisms Pol*(D) → Pol*(D') are available. The distinguished vertices are exactly the 'specializations' (images) of specialization vertices.

Hence the next question: are the specialization morphisms themselves deducible from the structures already in hand (graph, orientation, gradation, antipody)? The marginal note answers enthusiastically: 'mais oui, évidemment!'. The morphism is read on the deployed polygons. It suffices to know three things:
(a) that it respects the cyclic order;
(b) its effect on one of the two orientations, which is known;
(c) the image of one particular vertex (D,α) of P̂ol*(D). That image is known: it is the antipode, in P̂ol(D'), of the vertex (D',α).

Mathematically this is the rigidity of maps of cycles. A cyclic-order-preserving bijection between two n-cycles with prescribed orientation behaviour is fixed by the image of a single vertex. The dihedral group acts simply transitively on oriented pointed cycles.

Right column, second paragraph. A generalization is stated. Take a 2-cell of Γ (with boundary) whose three vertices have index 2, whose edges and corners have suitable indices, and in which the total gradation at each vertex (the sum of the gradations of the incident edges and corners) is constant. Then one gets 'transport isomorphisms' between the local polygons. These polygons form a local system on the surface underlying the cell.

In modern terms, the link polygons behave like a locally constant combinatorial sheaf over the 2-strata of a stratified cell complex. Specialization maps are transport or cospecialization maps of a constructible object. The next page then decides that the dual polygon (the boundary of a tubular neighbourhood, i.e. the disc Δ(D)) is 'le bon'.
errors: Not an error but a gap: claim (c), that the image of (D,α) is the antipode of (D',α), is asserted as 'known' without justification on this page.

The local-system claim for 2-cells is stated under hypotheses that are only partially legible (index conditions on edges and corners, constant total gradation). Monodromy triviality around the cell is not discussed. Since the cell is a disc this is automatic, but compatibility with the boundary edges is not checked.

Rigidity via (a)+(b)+(c) requires the map on deployed polygons to be a bijection, or at least a cyclic-order-preserving map of the same 'degree'. For specialization maps that collapse arcs (as suggested by the gradation-additivity of the previous page), one vertex plus orientation does not determine the map unless the gradations are also used. Grothendieck implicitly uses the deployed polygons to make this work, but this is not made explicit.

ideas.what: Local link polygon Pol*(D) of a vertex in the graph or complex of pseudo-line configurations, graded and with antipodal involution, and its 'deployed' version
ideas.modern_name: Link of a vertex / cell in a stratified (regular CW) complex; for pseudoline arrangements, the local structure of the poset of rank-3 oriented matroids under weak maps
ideas.usually_credited_to: Oriented matroid theory (Bland–Las Vergnas, Folkman–Lawrence 1978; Goodman–Pollack 1980s; MacPherson's combinatorial Grassmannian ~1993)

ideas.what: Specialization morphisms Pol*(D)→Pol*(D') are determined by cyclic order, effect on orientation, and the image of one distinguished vertex (the antipode of (D',α))
ideas.modern_name: Rigidity of dihedral-equivariant maps of cycles; cospecialization maps of a constructible sheaf

ideas.what: Local polygons over a 2-cell (three index-2 vertices, constant total gradation) form a local system with transport isomorphisms
ideas.modern_name: Locally constant (constructible) combinatorial sheaf on a stratum of an exit-path / stratified cell complex
ideas.usually_credited_to: MacPherson (exit paths, cellular sheaves), Treumann, Curry for cellular sheaves; in Grothendieck's own language, the 'tame topology' strata of the Esquisse
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) discusses tame topology / stratified structures and the 'Teichmüller tower' cell decompositions, but not this specific pseudo-line construction

missed.claim: Grothendieck aims at a purely combinatorial axiomatisation of the space of pseudo-line systems. The data are an oriented graded graph with link polygons, antipody and specialization maps, and these should be reconstructible from each other and form local systems over cells. This is a stratified-space / 'cellular sheaf' viewpoint on the moduli of pseudoline arrangements that was not carried through in his notes or, as far as known, in the oriented-matroid literature in this form.
missed.quote: on trouve des isos de transport entre les polygones locaux ... qui forment un syst. local sur la surface sous-jacente à la cellule !
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It links the combinatorics of rank-3 oriented matroids and pseudoline arrangements (MacPhersonian, mutation graphs) with the exit-path / constructible-sheaf description of stratified spaces. Such a link is natural today but rarely made explicitly for pseudoline moduli.

deep.surprise_reason: These are working notes with a modest observation: specialization maps are rigid and determined by orientation plus one vertex. There is also a sketch of a local-system structure over 2-cells. Both are conceptually in line with later stratified-space thinking, but they are elementary or incomplete and not a precise new result.

Line 6 likely reads 'qui correspondent à des triangles de pseudo-spécialisations'.
'les sommets de pr[?] spécialisation' is perhaps 'des pseudo-spécialisations'. The phrase 'comme les "spécialisations" de sommets de spécialisation' is followed by 'déjà connus' / 'décidables'.
Line 18: 'Mais bien sûr, via l'application correspondante des polygones déployés, car il suffit de savoir que [c'est] d'ordre (cyclique)'.

Right column, final paragraph: 'la gradation totale de chaque sommet (comme somme des gradations des arêtes et coins incidents) étant cste, on trouve des isos de transport entre les polygones locaux Pol*(E) qui forment un syst. local'. The reading 'diff^(E)' is likely 'Pol*(E)'.
